title: Reflection AI unveils Beam with lower-compute performance claims
dek: The Nvidia-backed company’s first open-weight model targets coding, reasoning and agentic tasks, with weights and technical documentation planned for October.
metaDescription: Reflection AI unveiled Beam, an open-weight model it says matches GLM-5.2 reasoning performance with less inference compute. Weights are due in October.

sections.heading: Beam’s pitch: comparable performance, less compute
sections.body:
Reflection AI has unveiled Beam, its first open-weight AI model, positioning it against Chinese open-weight competitors. The Nvidia-backed company says Beam offers performance comparable to Z.ai’s GLM-5.2, with lower computing requirements. Coding, reasoning and agentic tasks are the model’s stated areas of focus. [1][2][3]

The central efficiency claim comes from Reflection’s own evaluations: Beam performs comparably to GLM-5.2 on advanced reasoning benchmarks while using three to four times less inference compute. That attribution matters. The announcement presents a company-reported comparison, and the performance language should remain attached to Reflection’s evaluations rather than presented as an unqualified result. [1][3]

Beam’s positioning therefore combines two propositions: competitive results on the tasks Reflection is targeting, and less compute for the reasoning comparison it reports. For readers assessing the announcement, the useful distinction is between what the model is designed to do and what Reflection says its evaluations demonstrate. [1][2][3]

sections.heading: The model’s size and training
sections.body:
Beam has 501 billion total parameters and activates approximately 23 billion for a task. It uses a mixture-of-experts architecture. The comparison model, GLM-5.2, has approximately 744 billion total parameters and approximately 40 billion active parameters. Beam’s reported counts are lower on both measures, giving the announcement a concrete architectural comparison alongside its benchmark claims. [1][2][3]

Those figures should be kept separate from the claimed inference-compute reduction. Total parameters, active parameters and the reported compute comparison are three different parts of Reflection’s account. The parameter counts describe the models; the three-to-four-times-less-compute statement describes Reflection’s evaluation of Beam against GLM-5.2 on advanced reasoning benchmarks. [1][3]

Beam was pretrained on 23.8 trillion tokens, and its development involved large-scale reinforcement learning. These are the reported training details behind the model. They complement the size figures, but the claimed performance comparison still rests on the evaluations attributed to Reflection, not on the token count alone. [1][2][3]

sections.heading: Coding and agentic ambitions
sections.body:
Beyond advanced reasoning, Reflection says Beam is approaching Qwen3.8-Max’s capabilities in coding and agentic tasks. That is a separate comparison from the GLM-5.2 claim: the named reference model and the task categories differ. The wording also matters—“approaching” capabilities is not the same claim as matching them. [2][3]

The coding emphasis aligns with Reflection’s broader work developing tools aimed at automating software development. Beam’s stated focus on coding, reasoning and agentic tasks places the model within that effort. The announcement should therefore be read both as a first open-weight model unveiling and as part of the company’s software-development focus. [1][2][3]

Reflection was founded in 2024 by former DeepMind researchers Misha Laskin and Ioannis Antonoglou. Nvidia backs the company. These details establish who is behind Beam, while the technical case remains the model’s specifications and Reflection’s reported comparisons; the backing and founders are not substitutes for the performance evidence. [1][2][3]

sections.heading: The planned release is the next milestone
sections.body:
Reflection plans to release Beam’s weights and technical documentation in October. The release is a stated plan, distinct from the unveiling itself. For readers tracking availability, the precise takeaway is that Reflection has announced its first open-weight model and identified October as the planned window for publishing those materials. [1][3]

The company also signed an agreement with SpaceX for computing capacity earlier this year. That agreement provides capacity at Colossus 2. It is another part of Reflection’s development story, alongside Beam’s pretraining and reinforcement learning, but it is separate from the company’s claimed reduction in inference compute. [1][2][3]

The next milestone to watch is the planned weights-and-documentation release. The analytical question is whether Beam’s published technical account supports the combination Reflection is promoting: coding, reasoning and agentic capabilities, with comparable advanced-reasoning performance at lower inference compute. For now, keep the reported specifications, company evaluations and release plans clearly distinguished. [1][2][3]

keyTakeaways: Beam is Reflection AI’s first open-weight model, designed for coding, reasoning and agentic tasks. [1][2][3]
It has 501 billion total parameters and activates approximately 23 billion per task. [1][2][3]
Reflection’s evaluations claim comparable GLM-5.2 advanced-reasoning performance with three to four times less inference compute. [1][3]
Reflection plans to release the weights and technical documentation in October. [1][3]
whyItMatters: Beam’s proposition is comparable advanced-reasoning performance with lower inference compute, according to Reflection’s evaluations. [1][3] The key distinction is between that company-reported result, the model’s specifications and the planned October release of weights and technical documentation. [1][3]
